croydon-mayday: The "mayday" procedure word was conceived as a distress call in the early 1920s by Frederick Stanley Mockford, officer-in-charge of radio at Croydon Airport, England.
Since much of the air traffic at the time was between Croydon and Le Bourget Airport in Paris, he proposed the term "mayday", the phonetic equivalent of the French .
M'aider is literally the infinitive "to help me"
Following tests, the new procedure word was introduced for cross-Channel flights in February 1923.
Air traffic control was first developed here, as was the "Mayday" distress call.
The former terminal building is called Airport House, and the former control tower houses a visitors' centre.
crystal-palace-dinner: The models were unveiled in 1854, as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world.
To mark the launch of the models, Hawkins held a dinner on New Year's Eve 1853 inside the mould of one of the Iguanodon models.
An extensive restoration of the sculptures was completed in July 2026, which aimed to restore them to their original 1854 appearance.
chislehurst-bowie: Today the caves are a tourist attraction and, although they are called caves, they are entirely man-made and were dug and used as chalk and flint mines.
In the 1950s and 1960s, the caves were used as a skiffle and rock music venue.
David Bowie was known to have performed there four times: June 1962, 17 November 1962, in 1964 and 4 March 1966.
Jimi Hendrix played there twice: 16 December 1966 and 27 January 1967.
down-house-origin: The new billiard room was converted to a new study in 1881, and the old study where Darwin wrote On the Origin of Species was converted into a smoking room.

lesnes-becket: Lesnes Abbey, as it is now known, was founded by Richard de Luci, Chief Justiciar of England, in 1178.

This may have been in penance for his role in the protracted conflict between Henry II and Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury, which culminated in the latter's murder in 1170 by four of the king's knights.
red-house-wallpaper: Co-designed in 1859 by the architect Philip Webb and the designer William Morris, it was created to serve as a family home for Morris.
While at Red House, Morris was involved in the formation of his design company, Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., and embarked on his earliest wallpaper designs.
Red House would be Webb's first project as an independent architect, while it remained the only house that Morris ever built.
There was to be no wallpaper anywhere in the house, with the walls instead being painted or covered by tapestries.
upminster-sound: He produced the earliest reasonably accurate measurement of the speed of sound.
from 1689 to 1735 he was Rector at Upminster, Essex.
In 1709 Derham published a more accurate measure of the speed of sound, at 1,072 Parisian feet per second.

Derham used a telescope from the tower of the church of St Laurence, Upminster, to observe the flash of a distant shotgun being fired, and then measured the time until he heard the gunshot with a half second pendulum.
The tower of St Laurence's played a crucial role in Rev. William Derham's first accurate measurement of the speed of sound.
walthamstow-first-flight: In 1909, the aero-designer Alliott Verdon Roe made the first all-British powered flight across the marsh in a Roe I Triplane
A blue plaque records his achievement, on the railway arch in which he had his workshop.

there is now a blue plaque commemorating his first successful flight (in July 1909) at the site.
enfield-bren-sten: The Royal Small Arms Factory (RSAF), also known by the metonym Enfield, was a UK government-owned rifle factory in Enfield, adjoining the Lee Navigation in the Lea Valley.
Almost all the weapons in which the Royal Small Arms Factory had a hand in design or production carry either the word Enfield or the letters EN in their name
*Bren (Brno + Enfield), .303 Light machine gun from 1935 onwards.
*Sten (Shepherd, Turpin + Enfield) 9mm Sub-machine gun from 1941 to 1953
nonsuch-debts: Nonsuch Palace was a Tudor royal palace, commissioned by Henry VIII in Surrey, England, and on which work began in 1538.
Within two months the name "Nonsuch" appears in the building accounts, its name a boast that there was no such palace elsewhere equal to it in magnificence.
The palace remained standing until 1682–3, when it was pulled down by Barbara, Countess of Castlemaine, mistress to Charles II, to sell off building materials to pay for her gambling debts.
Its site lies in what is now Nonsuch Park on the boundary of the borough of Epsom and Ewell (in Surrey) and the London Borough of Sutton.

hounslow-baseline: The eventual mapping of the whole of the United Kingdom by the Ordnance Survey began with the measuring of an accurate base-line on Hounslow Heath, chosen for its flatness and its relative proximity to the Royal Greenwich Observatory.
Roy's first task (1784) was to measure a baseline between Hampton Poor House () and King's Arbour () on Hounslow Heath, a distance of just over 5 miles (8 km).
uxbridge-so-few: The Battle of Britain Bunker is an underground operations room at RAF Uxbridge, formerly used by No. 11 Group Fighter Command during the Second World War.
The floor of the Bunker is 60 ft underground and is accessed by a staircase of 76 steps.
The prime minister, Winston Churchill, visited the bunker on 16 August 1940 and spoke the famous words "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed, by so many, to so few".
